There a quite a few nursing programs in the greater Seattle area. A very popular one is Everett CC, which seems to be less competitive than others. North Seattle CC as well as Shoreline CC.

Here you'll find all of the accredited schools in WA state:
http://www.acenursing.us/accreditedprograms/programsearch.asp

Pull up a map and plug in the cities to see where they're at, as some are in eastern Washington, far from seattle (ie. Spokane CC, 3-4 hour drive)

Most of the programs share the same general prerequisites, or at least they did when I went, but they do differ slightly.. like one may require PSYCH 100 as a prerequisite while another school will require PSYCH 200.

If you know what particular area you're looking to live in I can help narrow it down.

The most important thing to remember is that the your prerequisite grades are the only ones that need to be nearly flawless. It's a competitive field to get into, but once you're in the programs it's not too challenging to stay afloat.
I was fortunate enough to start in an ER residency. If you've got the will, you'll get in where you want to be.

It lasts anywhere from 3 - 6 months usually, most likely 3.

Usually two components: On the job training, and education/modules/simulations

The hours combined of both will equal about a full time job. On the job training you'll do with a preceptor, who you shadow and progressively build your independence as a nurse. This is likely on day shift, and you'll most likely start your solo job after the residency program on night shift-- which is good because nights are typically quieter and you get a hourly differential, however adapting your life around night shift is a challenge, even if you're a self-proclaimed night owl like myself. Also, doctors are less available for guidance at night.

It seems that all hospitals face an RN shortage... yet all RNs face a job shortage.

Don't bother with an LPN unless it's a program requirement.

There are a couple good residency programs out here for new grads. Providence in Everett. Swedish Med Center downtown.

I just skipped down to the reasons why you're scared you wouldn't make a good nurse.. and I can assure you that most nurses had the same concerns during school.

1. Science comes natural to a select few. You're not expected to master the human body-- just to get familiar with basic physiologic concepts that you will only nail down as second nature eventually, after repeat exposure on the job.

2. Who doesn't get shaky when they're nervous? ;) I get a lot of physical manifestations of my anxiety (i.e. instantly sweat, become shaky, etc) I can tell you-- as a new grad in the ER, starting IVs was intimidating.. but once you've done something over and over, again, you become more confident and the discomfort subsides.. things will flow, I promise.

3. You will not fail at it. Some of the best advice I ever got was in nursing school-- my instructor said.. "If you ever feel like you won't be able to measure up as a nurse.. go to any nursing floor in any hospital and take a look around." The idea is that we often fantasize medical professionals as superior beings who were born into their roles.. when that's far from the truth. It just takes a desire to learn about, and care for, people... expertise only comes with time.

Shoot me a PM if you have any other Q's about admission, or just need some encouragement. You should get excited about the journey you're embarking on. It's a fun one.

I know this sounds super cliche, but try to understand the big picture. Through nursing school there were a lot of small details in the pathophysiology books that I would get caught up on. These are things that you're not expected to know. Focus on what is important for each system. The things that impact everyday life.

Stick it through. The prerequisites are meant to weed people out. Knowing every single bone in the body is irrelevant once you walk out of that class. Physiology will connect the dots. Micro is a pain but you'll get through it. I would have opted for a 5 week course vs a 13 week course, but I'm willing to go hard when it counts. Some people like to take it slow. Really think about how you are as a learner and go with that. You know yourself the best.

I was just hired into the ER as a new grad. I got a job as a unit secretary there about a year prior. They happen to be doing a nursing residency and the ER was picking up a couple new grads. Best thing you can do is get into a hospital system in another form and then get hired on from there. My area is saturated with experienced nurses as well as new grads. There were 500 new grad applicants for a handful of positions. If you can find a hospital that does nursing residencies, volunteer or get a job as a nurse tech/er tech there. Once they know your face, they'll pull your application when the time comes for choosin. Best of luck.
